messages.subject: Another CPO question!
parts:
I've run a besag / poisson model, in essence disease cases per population with a variety of covariates. There are 347 census units, many of which have 0 counts. The poisson model gives a better DIC / WAIC than a variety of other likelihoods. I've added random effects for three levels of spatial nesting, but I only have covariates for the lowest level (pictured).

Clearly there's great heterogeneity in the disease incidence (which is the whole purpose of the study).

But there's also heterogeneity of the CPO values -- seems like the model fits terribly in the places with the highest disease incidence. How would I explain that? I'm assuming this is analagous to residual clustering as we'd see in spatial regression?

messages.author: 9940b4fcc153c7d7
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Another CPO question!
parts:
It could be because the data is "overdispersed", which could be fixed by adding an iid random effect over the entire dataset.

Please check the $cpo$failures also, my experience is that this may be bad for these kinds of data.

Kind regards,
Haakon Bakka

parts:
Thanks, Haakon. I do have "iid" terms for block groups (the smallest spatial unit), tracts, and counties in this model:

form0<-cases ~ Pop +
  f(idx, model="besag", graph=adj)+
  f(tract, model="iid")+
  f(bg, model="iid") +
  f(county, model="iid")

model0 <- inla(form0, data = df, family='poisson',
               control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
               control.compute = list(dic = TRUE, waic = TRUE, cpo = TRUE))

There are a number of failures (yellow areas):

[1] 154.7137

messages.author: 9940b4fcc153c7d7
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Another CPO question!
parts:
You probably need to re-think your priors. With a complex model, the priors are very important!

With 154 failures, I do not think that any of the model comparison tools work. They give you a number, but I think those numbers make little sense. Does someone know this?

You can look at measures of fit, after computing the posterior distributions for $y_i$, i.e. checking how many observations end up in the different quantiles.

You can also do predictions, with hold-out sets, re-running the model several times.

Haakon
